U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin flew on a government jet to attend the Texas-LSU football game on Saturday, a day after a nationwide FAA system failure caused nearly 7,000 flight cancellations and 8,000 delays. 
Mullin watched the game from the private box of Ben Bordelon, whose company holds billions of dollars in DHS contracts, including a recent $2.2 billion icebreaker deal. 
DHS said Mullin was required to use a government aircraft for security reasons, paid for the personal trip and complied with ethics rules.
Source: New York Post

⚡️ 🇮🇱 The Israeli arms manufacturer Rafael Advanced Defense Systems has unveiled a new long‑range cruise missile called “SUPER ICE,” designed to penetrate modern air defense systems and carry out long‑distance strikes.
According to a report in the Israeli newspaper Maariv, development of the missile family began in 2021, after former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett discovered that the Israeli armed forces lacked operational plans and specialized munitions to strike Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.
In response, Bennett instructed the defense industry to accelerate the production of deep‑strike capabilities, which led to the creation of the ICE system, a cruise missile that can be launched from air, land, and sea platforms.
The upgraded SUPER ICE version features increased range, higher speed, and a warhead weighing 454 kg (1,000 pounds).
The report notes that earlier versions of the “ICE” missile have already been used operationally in attacks on Iran, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, and Qatar.

🚨 Why Mecca pact could further destabilize Syria and drag it deeper into regional conflicts
Syria is set to join the Mecca Pact that was formed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey. While the move could open up new opportunities for Damascus, it also carries significant risks, international observers warn.
🌏 Joining the military alliance could help Syria strengthen its legitimacy and standing within the Middle Eastern security architecture in the aftermath of the civil war
🌏 It could also bolster Syria's military capabilities and deepen its partnerships with influential regional powers through intelligence sharing, military training and financial support
🌏 The alliance could potentially also serve as a shield against further [Israeli land grabs in southwestern Syria ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77886)
Ground troops to fight the Houthis
Syria was invited to join the Mecca Pact primarily because Saudi Arabia needs ground forces to [fight Ansar Allah (the Houthis), experts say. Estimates](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77409) of the potential Syrian deployment range from 600 special forces personnel to as many as 20,000 troops. Various reports claim that a significant contingent has already been deployed to Saudi Arabia, although Damascus has denied the reports.
Notably, on November 4, Syrian de facto leader Ahmed al-Sharaa visited Riyadh and signed [six loan agreements worth $403 million](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77345).
Saudi Arabia reportedly began seeking Syria's [military assistance](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75882) as early as October 6. Although al-Sharaa had previously rejected a US proposal for Syria to fight Hezbollah in Lebanon, he appears to have agreed to Riyadh's request. Turkey had previously used Syrian fighters as proxies in Libya, while Al Jazeera reported that Syrians also took part in Azerbaijan's 2020 war against Armenia.
Nevertheless, Foreign Policy, Al-Monitor and other outlets warn that al-Sharaa was making a grave mistake that could come at the cost of his country.
🔴 Syria's "fractured and under-equipped military" is unlikely to change the course of the war in Yemen
🔴 A deployment could expose Damascus to retaliation not only from Ansar Allah and its network of allies, but potentially from the wider Axis of Resistance
🔴 It could undermine al-Sharaa's promise to keep Syria out of foreign conflicts and jeopardize the country's economic recovery
🔴 Most Syrians view Israel as a major threat, not the Yemenis. Moreover, they have not forgotten how Gulf states funded ISIS and al-Qaeda affiliates during the Syrian civil war, while Turkish forces looted Syrian industrial equipment and burned agricultural fields.

events.text:
🤝 Why Europe resists a Ukraine peace deal and new security order with Russia
The EU has criticized US-Russia peace talks on Ukraine and pledged to deploy troops there once hostilities end – a move that could reignite the conflict. So does Europe want peace?
Some economic commentators point to “Military Keynesianism” — using billions in defense spending to stimulate a waning economy under the pretext of an imminent security threat.
Europe's energy crisis, coupled with weakening demand, growing competition from China, the costs of its green transition, sanctions on Russia and, more recently, US tariffs, has accelerated de-industrialization across the bloc, particularly in Germany, its industrial powerhouse.
In October 2025, the EU unveiled its ambitious ReArm Europe Plan/Readiness 2030, envisaging €800 billion ($881 billion) in additional defense spending.
Why five years? Because while such spending will fuel public debt in the short term, its proponents expect it to pay off over time. The perceived Russian threat must remain central throughout this period: it's the key justification for the bloc’s relentless military spending.
Why Europe is embracing Military Keynesianism
🔴 Government funding for arms production can boost aggregate demand, create jobs and stimulate economic activity, particularly when financed through additional public spending
🔴 Defense contracts can absorb idle industrial capacity, put underused facilities and workers back to work, and generate wages without flooding consumer markets with goods or directly competing with private businesses
🔴 Military equipment requires regular maintenance, upgrades and replacement. It can also be destroyed or depleted in conflict, creating recurring procurement orders
🔴 Politically, security threats make it easier for governments to justify rapid increases in defense production and borrowing
Germany is a glaring example: it is re-purposing a struggling transport sector for military production. For instance:
🔴 Volkswagen has agreed to sell its Osnabruck plant to Aurelius for [air defense production with Israel’s Rafael ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71037)
🔴 Alstom’s former rail plant in Gorlitz has been converted into a defense production site by KNDS
🔴 Schaeffler has struck a deal with [defense technology firm Helsing ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/58892)to scale up drone production.
Similar shifts are underway across the EU, with billions pouring into defense contracts. A Ukraine peace deal or a lasting European security framework could undermine this momentum by removing Russia as a convenient security threat – and [jeopardizing the interests built around it.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77866)
Meanwhile, economists warn that Military Keynesianism comes with significant risks for Europe, including structural problems, soaring inflation and a potential debt crisis.

🚀 CENTCOM is scrambling for concrete bunkers after Iran's strikes on US bases
As the conflict with Iran drags on, the Pentagon is facing a grim reality: US soldiers deployed across the Middle East have been sheltering in converted steel shipping containers this entire time.
The Army just posted a contracting notice demanding 17 reinforced concrete bunkers: 10 in Israel, 5 in Saudi Arabia, and 2 in Lebanon, the War Zone reported.
Companies are being given only 8 days to respond and 3 days to quote a price, with a mandatory construction window of just 45 days.
Earlier in the war, [six American soldiers were killed in Kuwait](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75826) when an Iranian drone struck an operations center set up inside a converted trailer.
This urgent bunker scramble comes just [days before a 60 Minutes interview](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77832) airs with the families of those killed, raising questions about why basic force protection wasn't provided.
